Farida was alone at the pharmacy counter on the night shift when a man pushed to the front, shouting that his prescription had been filled wrong. She started to explain. He slammed his fist on the glass, then again, harder. "Come out here and say that!" He was shaking with rage and moving towards the side door.
Farida's heart hammered. This was not a conversation anymore.
She stopped talking, stepped back from the counter, and walked into the locked back room. She pressed the alarm button and called the hospital security desk. "Pharmacy, man threatening staff, please come now."
Within two minutes Sachin, the security guard, and a colleague arrived. The man was led out. Security called the police to record it.
Later, Sachin sat with her while she drank water, her hands still trembling. "You did the right thing, not arguing," he said. "We'll have two people on nights from tomorrow."

qa.a: She pressed the alarm button.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when the man slammed the glass?
qa.a: Farida was frightened, her heart hammering, and she realised reasoning with him was no longer safe.

qa.q: Which choices kept Farida safe, and why?
qa.a: She stopped arguing, put a locked door between them and called security at once, putting safety before any explanation.

qa.q: How did Sachin respond to what happened?
qa.a: Sachin came quickly, stayed with Farida while she calmed down, reassured her she did the right thing and promised two staff on nights.

Neelam was parking her scooter in the Pune society when Uday from the third floor came storming down. "That's my spot! How many times do I have to tell you people?" His face was red. He kicked her scooter's wheel.
"Uday, it's the visitors' spot, I checked—"
He stepped closer and raised his fist. "Say one more word."
Neelam's stomach dropped. She didn't finish the sentence. She stepped back, turned, and walked quickly to the security cabin at the gate, not looking back.
"Bhaiya, he's threatening me. Please stay here with me." The guard stood beside her and called the society secretary.
Neelam called her friend to come over, then called the police helpline and reported it. Her voice shook, but she said every detail.
That evening the secretary came to her door. "We've written it in the complaint book, and we'll talk to Uday with the committee present. Not alone."

qa.a: She walked quickly to the security cabin at the gate.

I'm Vandana, and I'll never forget the week Kavitha, my ten-year-old, told me every night that her maths homework was done. "Done, Amma." Then the teacher's note came: five pages missing.
My first reaction was anger. I wanted to shout, "You lied to me!" But I looked at her face when I showed her the note. She went white and started crying before I'd said a word. She wasn't sneaky. She was terrified.
So I sat on the floor beside her. "Kavi, I'm not going to punish you for telling me the truth now. What's going on?"
She whispered that she didn't understand fractions and was scared I'd be disappointed.
We did the pages together that week. And we made a rule: if you're stuck, telling me is never trouble.
She tells me now, most of the time.

I'm Usha, Manoj's elder sister, and I was home from college the month he turned fifteen. I noticed our father noticing things too: Manoj flipping his phone face down at dinner, going to the terrace to take calls, saying "just friends" and nothing more.

Manoj shrugged, then said something about a boy from the football club. I couldn't hear all of it.
Then Papa said, "You don't have to tell me everything. But two rules: you never meet anyone from online without telling us, and if anything online scares you, you come to me. No trouble for telling."
I don't know what Manoj felt. But the next week I saw him show Papa a funny video from the football group.

In the school hostel, the Class 11 results were posted on the board on Friday. Dhruv had failed physics and would have to repeat the year.
On the phone that night, his mother asked, "Results?" He said, "Not out yet." On Sunday he said it again.
He stopped going to the common room, where everyone was talking about Class 12 subjects. He ate at odd hours to avoid his roommate, Omkar. At night he lay awake, heart racing, imagining his father's face.
Omkar finally caught him at the washbasins. "Dhruv, I saw the board. I'm not going to tell anyone. But you look awful."
Dhruv's eyes stung. "I haven't told my parents. I keep lying."
"Do you want to call them with me here? Or tell the warden first?"
Dhruv thought. "The warden. Then my parents. Today."
They walked to the warden's office together.

I'm writing this because I can't say it on the phone. I have to repeat Class 10.

I found out in May. I didn't tell you. I didn't tell anyone except my parents. When you asked about results, I said I was "waiting for the rechecking". There was no rechecking.

Hiding it felt safe for a week. Then it just felt lonely. Every message from you made my stomach hurt, because I'd have to lie again.

Will you still write to me?

Salma

Pema found out on a Tuesday, in their Delhi flat, that Jagdish had not told his parents about their engagement. For the third time. He had said, in March, "I told them, they're fine." In June: "They're coming around." Today his mother had called Pema by mistake and asked, puzzled, who she was.

I'm Jahnavi, and the year Joseph and I were together, he lied to me about where he was, again and again. "Late meeting." "Stuck at my cousin's." "Phone died." Small things, each one. I found out about the first one by accident, forgave it, then found another. By the fifth, I didn't know which of his words were real.

A friend gave me the number of a counsellor. Those sessions helped me untangle it: his lies were his choice, not my failure.
I told Joseph clearly: one more lie and I'm leaving. He lied again two weeks later.

I've noticed a pattern in Group B. Sharmila, a second-year student, begins a point and Ramesh talks over her before she finishes. Today it happened four times. Twice, Ramesh later repeated her idea about rural credit almost word for word, and the group credited him.

I stayed back with her afterwards. She said, "Maybe my English isn't clear enough." I told her it was clear; the problem was the interruptions.
She asked whether it would be rude to say, "Can I finish my point?" I said it is completely fair.
What I'll do next: I will start using a speaking order in Group B, and when an idea is repeated, I will name who said it first. I'll check in with Sharmila after next week's session.

Kavitha, one of our strongest designers, has always spoken the most in meetings: quick, full of ideas, often answering questions meant for others. Last month in her feedback, I mentioned that newer team members like Swati rarely spoke when she was in the room.
Kavitha took it seriously. In today's review she kept a small tally on her notepad: each time she spoke, one line. After four lines she stopped and asked, "Swati, you worked on the checkout flow. What did you notice?"
Swati hesitated, then gave the best observation of the meeting: users were abandoning the page at the address step.
After the meeting, Kavitha told me the tally felt silly at first but useful. "I didn't realise how much space I was taking."
What I will do next: I will ask Kavitha to mentor Swati on the checkout redesign.
